chunks.text: To write code, we have already defined an area of numbers
Now let's make a function
public static
We will keep its return type as int and name it as binary search
In binary search, first we will get an area named numbers
Apart from that, in our arguments, we will get another thing, our key
Now the pseudocode of binary search used to say, first make start and end
So let's make start and end
Start will be 0
End will be n-1
i.e. numbers.length-1
Now we have to run a loop
How will we run the loop?
Till our start is less than or equal to end
We have heard about start less than end
What is the logic behind equal to?
We have put equal to because
In that case, our area will be in the smallest size
i.e. start, mid and end will be the same
We will be comparing the key with a single element
That case will be when start is equal to end
First we will calculate mid
Mid is start plus end divided by 2
Now we will do comparisons
In comparisons, first of all, if numbers of mid is equal to key
In this case, we will return our mid
i.e. our key exists on this index
In the second case, if numbers of mid is less than key
In which case, our mid value is less than key
In that case, we will search in the second half
This was our right condition
So what will we update to search in the second half?
We will update start
Start will be mid plus 1
But if it is not equal to or less than
Then obviously it will be greater than
In that case, we will update
This will be our left case
i.e. first half
In this, we will update our end
End will be mid minus 1
Once we update our start and end
Then this cycle will start again
Loop will continue till our start is less than equal to end
In the last, we will return minus 1
Why did we return minus 1?
If our key exists in the array
Then at some point, this condition will be true
i.e. found condition
But if this condition is never true
And this limit is reached
If it is greater than start and end
In that case, we will return minus 1
i.e. our key does not exist in the array
Now let's search our key
System.out.println
Here we will write index for key is
We will call binary search
We have passed numbers in binary search
Now let's save this
So what is the index we got?
For our key, we got index 4
If we see in our array, then our key 10
Which index does it exist on?
It exists on our index 4
Now let's change the key a little
Let's make the key 4
Let's take out the index for 4
For 4, we will get index 1
0 and on 1, we have 4
Let's put a key which does not exist
Let's say 25
In this case, index print will be minus 1
And we know that minus 1 is an invalid index
Index starts from 0 in the array
So minus 1 index does not exist
Negative values do not exist for index
Now those students who have an idea of time complexity
For them, let me tell you
How do we calculate the time complexity of our binary search?
Let's see the iterations
That means how many times we searched our loop in our array
So iteration 1
When we entered the loop for the first time
The size of our array was n
The second time we entered, the size of the array became n by 2
The third time we entered, the size of the array became n by 4
The fourth time we entered, the size of the array became n by 8
In the same way, the size will decrease until the value of n becomes 1
So there is a mathematical formula to calculate this
Let's say n divided by
If you see all these, then there are powers of 2
Like this is n divided by 2 to the power 2
This is n divided by 2 to the power 1
This is n divided by 2 to the power 0
This is n divided by 2 to the power 3
And similarly, the value of n divided by 2 to the power k will become 1
So we have to subtract this k
Because this is our 0th iteration
This is our first iteration, this is our second iteration, this is our third iteration
In the same way, this will become our kth iteration
But if we have to consider it as first, second, third
Then this will be k plus 1th iteration
In which finally, we will get our mid in the worst case scenario
We will get our key
We have to take this as 1
That means n is equal to 2 to the power k
And k will become log of n base 2
This is our complexity
So our time complexity of this code will be directly proportional to log of n base 2
In fact, it will be big of log n
Here we don't write base 2 because it doesn't make much difference from base
So we say log n
That time complexity is log n in binary search
If you take log of any n on base 2
Then that value will always be less
What does this tell us?
This tells us that the time complexity of linear search
And the time complexity of binary search
In that, you can put any value of n
The time complexity of binary search will always be less
That means the code of binary search will always perform better
Because that code will be executed quickly
It will take less time
Let's take an example for an array
Let's take an array of 8 size
So the size of the array or n is equal to 8
In linear search, we have to check 8 elements
If that element doesn't exist in the array
So in this, it will be big of 8 time complexity
But what will happen in binary search?
First, we will check in 8 size
Then we will check in 4
Then we will check in 2
Then we will check in 1
So here our loop will run 4 times
So here it will be big of 4
So obviously binary search will perform better in this case
As compared to a linear search
